title: B2B GTM Maturity Score
subtitle: Measures how well your go-to-market engine is built to scale revenue without adding headcount proportionally.

questions.text: How would you describe the current state of your GTM setup?

answers.label: Marketing, sales, and ops run independently. Separate tools, separate data, minimal coordination.
Teams share a CRM but most processes and handoffs are still manual.
We have some automation and shared data, but attribution and reporting require manual work.
Most GTM signals flow between teams automatically. Lag is low but not eliminated.
GTM runs as one integrated system: data, tooling, sales, and ops feed each other without manual intervention.

questions.text: How quickly can your team validate a new GTM approach: new channel, new message, new play?

answers.label: Months. Budget approval and multiple stakeholder meetings come first.
4 to 8 weeks, when the team is aligned.
2 to 4 weeks with the resources we have today.
Under 2 weeks. We can spin up and read a signal quickly.
Days. Small test, clear signal, then we decide to scale or drop.

questions.text: When a buying signal comes in (high-intent visit, intent data spike, engagement from a target account), how does your team respond?

answers.label: We do not have visibility into those signals.
Someone manually checks the tools and alerts the right person when they remember to.
We have alerts set up, but follow-up is inconsistent.
Signals trigger automated workflows that route to the right rep or sequence.
Signals are scored, cross-referenced across tools, and routed automatically within minutes.

questions.text: How does your GTM strategy account for buying committees of 6 to 11 people making decisions together?

answers.label: We target one contact per account and rely on them to sell internally.
We know multi-stakeholder decisions happen but have no structured approach for them.
We map stakeholders per deal, but only after the first meeting.
We proactively map buying committees and build content for multiple roles.
We run multi-touch, multi-stakeholder plays before the first conversation. We are in the room before the meeting.

low.headline: Your GTM is a collection of tools, not a system.
low.text: B2B teams running 20 to 30 disconnected automations and calling it a strategy is the norm at this stage. The cost is not in the tools. It is in signal lag. Every hour a buying signal sits unactioned is an hour a competitor gets to that account first.
steps: Audit your current GTM tools and find the 3 biggest handoff gaps between marketing, sales, and ops.
Pick one buying signal (high-intent visit, competitor page view, ICP engagement) and build one automated response workflow for it this month.
Map your buying committee for your top 3 deal types before your next campaign runs: who is the champion, the economic buyer, the blocker.

mid.headline: You have the pieces. Now wire them together.
mid.text: You are not starting from zero. You have automation, you have data. The gap is that the pieces are not talking to each other yet. Teams at this stage often have the infrastructure to move fast. They just have not connected the loops.
steps: Map the full signal-to-response flow for your top two demand channels and find the first manual step that could be automated.
Cut your validation cycle in half: pick one GTM test this quarter and run it in 10 days instead of your usual timeline.
Build a buying committee playbook for your core ICP: at minimum, who the champion, economic buyer, and blocker typically are.

high.headline: You are running a revenue engine, not a marketing department.
high.text: This is where GTM becomes a compounding advantage. The question is not whether you are fast. It is whether the system keeps improving. The teams that win long-term treat GTM architecture as a product they ship, test, and refine continuously.
steps: Document your GTM architecture so the system does not depend on any one person to run it.
Add one new signal type or data layer this quarter: intent data, AI search visibility, or dark-funnel tracking.
Run a GTM retrospective every 6 weeks: what did the system learn, what do you retire, what do you scale?

questions.text: When GenAI flooded your market with templated content and templated outbound, how did your content strategy respond?

answers.label: It did not. We are still publishing the same type of content on the same schedule.
We slowed down publishing but have not changed the approach.
We are moving toward more specific, data-backed content but have not fully committed.
We repositioned around POV-driven content: who says it matters as much as what is said.
Authority is the primary differentiator. Buyers find us through credibility, not volume.

questions.text: How does your company build credibility and generate demand in your market?

answers.label: Mainly through our website, paid ads, and case studies.
Word of mouth and founder networks, mostly unstructured.
Some thought leadership content, but it is inconsistent and not tied to pipeline.
Active founder-led content and B2B influencer relationships drive a share of pipeline.
Founder-led selling and owned authority are primary demand drivers. Buyers come to us before we reach them.

questions.text: How does your current strategy account for AI search (GEO and AEO) as a discovery channel?

answers.label: It does not. We are focused on traditional SEO.
We know it matters but have not changed how we create or structure content.
We are experimenting with formats that show up in AI-generated answers.
We have audited our content for AI search visibility and made structural changes to how we publish.
GEO and AEO are core parts of our content and SEO strategy with dedicated testing and measurement.

low.headline: Volume without authority is noise.
low.text: The playbooks that worked 3 years ago are dead. GenAI dropped content production cost to near zero. Publishing more of the same is now the minimum requirement for being ignored. The teams winning are building credibility, not output. One credible voice now outperforms a full content team publishing templated posts.
steps: Audit your last 10 pieces of content: would a buyer trust it more because of who wrote it, or is it interchangeable with what your competitors publish?
Pick one senior voice in your company (founder, CMO, or domain expert) and build a consistent publishing rhythm for them on LinkedIn.
Run a basic GEO audit: search for 5 questions your ideal buyer asks before they buy and check whether you appear in the AI-generated answers.

mid.headline: You are moving in the right direction. Now connect it to pipeline.
mid.text: You have a POV and some credibility-building in motion. The gap most teams face at this stage is that the content strategy is not tied directly to demand and pipeline. Thought leadership that does not generate named leads or booked conversations is a branding exercise, not a GTM play.
steps: Add a demand capture layer to your top-performing content: a specific next step tied to the audience's decision, not a generic contact form.
Map your content to your buying committee: are you building content for the economic buyer, not just the practitioner?
Test one GEO-optimized piece this quarter: structured, specific, answering a question your ICP actively searches before they buy.

high.headline: Authority is your advantage. Now make it compound.
high.text: When who said it matters more than what was said, you are ahead of most B2B teams. The next move is turning the audience you built into a pipeline engine that runs independently of campaign spend.
steps: Build a content-to-pipeline attribution model: track which pieces of content appear in the journey of your closed deals.
Add a B2B influencer or co-creation layer to your strategy to amplify credibility through adjacent voices in your market.
Treat GEO and AEO as a primary channel, not an experiment. Allocate dedicated budget and measurement for one full quarter.

questions.text: When you present marketing results to your CEO or CFO, what metric drives the conversation?

answers.label: Marketing Qualified Leads (MQLs) or lead volume.
Meetings booked or opportunities created by marketing.
Pipeline value influenced by marketing-sourced deals.
Revenue influenced by marketing across the full funnel, with an attribution model behind it.
Marketing's contribution to closed revenue. The conversation starts and ends in euros.

questions.text: How confident are you in your pipeline attribution: knowing which channels and campaigns actually drive revenue?

answers.label: We cannot reliably connect marketing spend to pipeline or closed revenue.
We use last-touch attribution. We know it is incomplete.
We have multi-touch attribution but leadership does not fully trust the model.
We have a clear view of which channels drive pipeline, and the team makes budget decisions based on it.
Leadership uses the attribution model to allocate budget. It is trusted, not just tracked.

questions.text: How many hours per week does your team spend on manual GTM reporting and attribution: pulling data, building slides, reconciling numbers across tools?
questions.hint: Count all time: marketing ops, demand gen lead, and your own prep for leadership reporting.

questions.text: What is the all-in hourly cost (gross salary plus overhead) of the person doing most of that reporting work?
questions.hint: Quick estimate: monthly gross salary multiplied by 1.5 for overhead, divided by 168 working hours.

low.headline: MQLs do not control the budget. Revenue does.
low.text: I have sat in enough boardrooms to know that 'marketing generated X leads' does not land. CEOs nod. Then they ask about revenue. Proving marketing's value as a revenue function is the work. Better reporting alone will not get you there.
steps: Stop reporting MQLs to leadership. Replace that metric with pipeline sourced and revenue influenced by marketing, even if the initial number is smaller.
Build a simple attribution model for your top 3 acquisition channels: even last-touch is better than no attribution.
Map one closed deal back to its first marketing touch and bring that path to your CEO or CFO in the next review.

mid.headline: You have the data. Now make leadership trust it.
mid.text: Attribution data that leadership does not trust is as useful as no data. The gap at this stage is usually one of two things: the model is right but the story is not told clearly, or the model has known gaps that have not been addressed. Either way, the fix is the same: close the gap and bring the evidence.
steps: Run a closed-deal audit: pick your last 10 closed-won deals and trace the full marketing touch sequence for each.
Present attribution data alongside a specific business outcome: not 'we drove 30 opportunities,' but 'three of the four deals that closed this quarter touched this campaign first.'
Identify the one attribution gap generating the most skepticism from leadership and address it this quarter.

high.headline: Revenue-fluent marketing changes the budget conversation.
high.text: When marketing proves its value in euros, budget conversations shift. You stop defending the function and start allocating capital. The next move is using attribution confidence to make smarter bets: scaling what compounds and cutting what only looks good on a slide.
steps: Build a 12-month pipeline forecast driven by marketing inputs and show leadership where pipeline will come from before it exists.
Add customer revenue expansion to your attribution model: marketing's contribution does not stop at closed-won.
Turn your reporting cadence into a decision loop: every review ends with one allocation decision, not just a recap.

questions.text: How does your team currently use AI across GTM execution?

answers.label: Writing assistance and basic content generation. That is about it.
A few specific tasks are automated: email sequences, data enrichment, or basic lead scoring.
AI runs 3 to 5 key workflows: scoring, enrichment, content, or reporting.
Most repetitive GTM tasks run on AI-assisted workflows. The team focuses on decisions, not execution.
Our GTM stack runs on interconnected AI systems. One person now outputs what used to take a full team.

questions.text: How does your team decide which AI tools or approaches to adopt?

answers.label: We try tools as they get popular, mostly based on what shows up in our feed.
Someone on the team champions a tool and others follow when capacity allows.
We evaluate tools against specific use cases before rolling them out.
We have a structured evaluation process tied to GTM outcomes and team capacity.
We validate new AI approaches in days: test, read the signal, integrate or drop. Validation speed is itself an advantage.

questions.text: How is your revenue operations (RevOps) function structured today?

answers.label: No dedicated RevOps function. Everyone does a bit of it.
RevOps tasks are spread across marketing, sales, and ops: whoever has time handles them.
One person owns RevOps, but mostly reactively: fixing problems rather than building systems.
RevOps is a proactive function building and improving the revenue system on a defined roadmap.
RevOps, marketing ops, and sales ops are unified into one team running the full revenue engine.

questions.text: When you think about scaling revenue over the next 12 months, what is your primary approach?

answers.label: Hiring more salespeople and marketers.
Increasing spend on the channels that already work.
A mix of headcount and improved tooling, with no clear priority between them.
Mostly tooling and process improvement. Headcount scales when the system is ready for it.
The system scales first. We build revenue infrastructure that multiplies the output of the team we already have.

low.headline: AI as a writing tool is the floor, not the ceiling.
low.text: Most teams at this stage are using AI for content and calling it transformation. The real work is in the workflow layer: scoring, enrichment, routing, reporting. One person with the right AI stack can now ship what took a full team 6 months ago. The question is whether you are building that stack or watching others do it.
steps: Pick one repetitive GTM task your team does every week and build an AI workflow for it this month. Start with the most time-consuming, lowest-judgment task.
Audit your current tool stack: which tools overlap, which do not connect to each other, and which could be replaced by one AI-assisted workflow?
Find one AI-native GTM team in your industry and map out what their stack likely looks like. That is your benchmark.

mid.headline: You are building the stack. Now make it compound.
mid.text: Three to five integrated workflows is real progress. Most teams are not there. The shift now is from individual workflow automation to interconnected systems where one signal triggers a chain of actions. That is where the output gap between your team and a headcount-heavy competitor starts to show up.
steps: Map the connections between your existing AI workflows: what should trigger what, and which handoffs are still manual?
Test one multi-step AI play this quarter: a signal from one system automatically triggers actions in two others without manual intervention.
Document the AI systems you have built so they survive team changes. A workflow no one else understands is a liability.

high.headline: You are running the GTM model most teams are still planning.
high.text: When your GTM stack runs as an interconnected system, every person you add has a multiplied output. The teams that stay here do not coast. They keep the validation loop tight, retire what stops working, and add new AI layers before competitors catch up.
steps: Measure your AI GTM system output per headcount. This is the number that makes the internal case for the next system you build.
Find the next workflow layer you have not built yet: customer expansion, competitive monitoring, or partner channel automation.
Run a quarterly AI stack audit: retire tools that no longer add signal and put that budget toward the next experiment.

cta.headline: Want a partner who turns this score into an actual plan?
cta.description: Most people don't fail at the assessment. They fail at sequencing. In 30 minutes I'll show you which two things to fix first, based on your score and your stage. No pitch deck, just the sequencing call.
